# A3. Identification of X {#arg-leisure}

The paper takes the taste for leisure $X$ common to the four formal income quartiles and pins its level by the
average formal workweek, so that relative hours across the quartiles are a prediction. The alternative takes the
survey's relative hours as data and identifies one $X_i$ per quartile, which leaves the level of hours
unidentified. The two calibrations share their targets, $\beta$, $\omega$ and every equilibrium outcome of section
{{< var p.sec_argentina >}}: the tax rate, savings, hours in efficiency units and the reform at every ρ. The reason
is that the productivity distribution reaches the aggregates only through
$\sum_{i>0}\gamma_i\eta_i^{1+\xi}/X_i^{\xi}$, which both calibrations normalize to one (appendix
{{< var p.app_EPH >}}). The tables below therefore show only what differs.

## The calibration {#arg-leisure-calibration}

Four rows of the paper's calibration table differ. In the survey, hours rise less with income than the common $X$
predicts: the top quartile works fewer hours than predicted, as section {{< var p.sec_argentina >}} notes, and the
others a little more. The vector $X_i$ take those hours as data, so the taste for leisure rises with income, and the
productivities spread further apart to reproduce the same relative incomes. The informal productivity and taste for leisure are measured against
the formal average and move with it.

{{< include _generated/exhibits/ARG_LeisureCalibration.qmd >}}

## Why the level of $X$ differs {#arg-leisure-level}

The level of the taste for leisure is not comparable across the two calibrations. Under the common $X$ it is the
unit in which hours are measured: it is set so that average formal hours in the model equal the observed workweek,
and every productivity scales with it. Under the vector $X_i$ the survey's relative hours fix only the ratios of the
$X_i$, and the unit of hours is a normalization, which sets the level of every $X_i$, of the productivities and of
the informal taste for leisure. Since that level enters no aggregate, nothing else moves. Across the IES, the
common $X$ falls a little as ρ rises, because average hours are matched against a slightly different equilibrium
at each ρ, while the informal parameters barely move under either calibration.
